newsitem.title: USA: Clinton names Tenet his choice to head CIA.
newsitem.headline: Clinton names Tenet his choice to head CIA.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Wednesday turned to acting CIA Director George Tenet to head the spy agency permanently, a move expected to avoid the political clash that derailed his first choice for the job.
Clinton hailed his new choice as someone who "brings a wealth of experience and skill to the challenge of leading our intelligence community into the 21st century."

Tenet, 44, who was deputy CIA director before his interim appointment as acting director last December, replaces Anthony Lake, who withrew from consideration on Monday after withering Senate confirmation hearings.

"If confirmed, I will do my level best to provide leadership, stability and strength of purpose to the fine men and women who serve our nation with such devotion," said Tenet, sending a message to an agency troubled by scandals and changes in leadership.
Tenet, a close friend of Lake's, was unlikely to encounter similar stiff opposition in winning Senate confirmation.

Sen. Richard Shelby, Republican chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee and a nemisis of the Lake nomination, quickly praised Tenet as "a man of integrity and professionalism. He has a distinguished record of service in the intelligence community."

Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott also appeared pleased by the choice of Tenet. "This looks like a good choice," he said. "I look forward to meeting Mr. Tenet soon and I expect rapid Senate confirmation."
Clinton said he wanted quickly to name a new choice to head the CIA because of the importance of the job. "You can't have a ship without a captain," he said.
But Tenet may yet run into trouble, according to a CBS News report on Wednesday night.

The network reported that a former State Department official whose security clearance was revoked by Tenet over accusations he revealed CIA secrets to The New York Times suspects that it was Tenet himself who revealed the secrets.
"What he's doing is sitting in judgment on me about an issue of which I believe he is, in fact, guilty," Richard Nuccio told CBS "60 Minutes" program last November.

CBS' Mike Wallace reported that on Wednesday afternoon he had "reconfirmed that George Tenet had in fact given the CIA secrets to The New York Times, something that Tenet absolutely denies," and that Tenet was aided on this by Nancy Soderberg, who was Lake's No. 3 at the National Security Council.
The network further reported that White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton was aware of Nuccio's accusations and is confident that Tenet did nothing wrong.
Tenet served as staff director of the Senate Intelligence Committee, which anchors the confirmation process, and he underwent scrutiny when confirmed by the Senate as deputy CIA director.
Among other previous key posts in Washington, Tenet also worked at the White House from 1993 until 1995 as chief intelligence adviser to Lake, who was Clinton's national security adviser.
He crafted presidential directives on intelligence priorities, security coordination, spy-catching and satellite remote-sensing policies.
His Capitol Hill experience came as staff director on the Senate Intelligence Committee from 1988-93.
Lake abruptly ended his own quest for confirmation as CIA director on Monday after a combative three-month process that he said was more than he could bear.

Lake said he feared the agency and his own integrity would be damaged by the prolonged pounding from Republican senators on issues ranging from his knowledge of questionable White House fund-raising practices to his management of the National Security Council staff, his failure to divest himself of some stock and his role in U.S. policy in Bosnia.
Critics led by Shelby, an Alabama Republican, said they were pursuing legitimate lines of inquiry as to whether Lake was competent to manage the gigantic, sprawling U.S. intelligence community.
Its components, the CIA and 12 sister spy agencies, employ about 80,000 people, according to Shelby, and currently spend about $30 billion a year.
